41.text: Latency is the whole point. We care about time-to-first-token and throughput because serving architecture is judged by user-visible delay, not by elegance.

258.text: The dense per-token work: four attention projections, two MLP matmuls at 4x width, and the output head. All of it is strictly linear in token count, which is exactly why counting attention alone gets the exponent wrong.

259.text: The only quadratic term. Causal masking leaves T^2/2 query-key pairs, each costing 2 * n_embd for the score and 2 * n_embd for the value-weighted sum.

260.text: Prefill total = linear dense work + quadratic attention. Which term dominates depends entirely on T, and the printed attention-share column is what makes the crossover visible instead of assumed.

262.text: Decode's attention cost grows with the context it attends over, so it is summed per step rather than taken as a single T^2 term.

Reading the total alone hides both effects.

344.text: Simulated prefill cost per prompt token. Deliberately in the milliseconds: on a loaded host time.sleep() overshoots by around a millisecond, so a simulation built on 0.3 ms sleeps would measure OS scheduling noise instead of its own cost model. Only the ratios between these three constants matter.

345.text: Simulated decode cost per step, lower than prefill's per-token cost. Decode does less arithmetic per token; on real hardware it is memory-bound instead.

353.text: The one cost disaggregation adds and colocated serving never pays. In this lab the handoff is a tuple of the same tensors on a queue, with no copy at all, so without an explicit charge the simulation would report the transfer as free while the closing text says it costs a millisecond. Charge it, then print the break-even value.

371.text: Each request carries its own sampling RNG. The global torch RNG is unusable here: the disaggregated arm samples from two threads, so thread interleaving decides who draws which number and the generated names changed from run to run. Per-request generators make both strategies draw the same numbers in the same order for the same request, so the text is identical by construction and only latency differs.

374.text: Create a realistic workload: mix of short prompts (fast prefill) and long prompts (slow prefill). The long prompts are the problem, they block everything in colocated serving.

421.text: Colocated serving: one worker does both prefill and decode. Requests are handled FIFO, so a long prefill blocks every request behind it.

423.text: Handle one request at a time in FIFO order: prefill its prompt, then decode all tokens before moving to the next.

442.text: Disaggregated serving: separate prefill and decode workers connected by a queue, so prefill does not block decode. The key insight is that while one worker prefills a long prompt, the other keeps decoding in-flight requests.

443.text: Thread-safe queue connects prefill worker to decode worker.

444.text: Results collection with lock for thread safety.

458.text: Ship the KV cache before recording the first-token time. The first token is not useful until the request can actually continue on the decode worker, so the transfer belongs inside TTFT rather than outside it.

459.text: Record time-to-first-token, which now depends only on this request's prefill rather than on the requests before it.

460.text: Push the prefilled request state onto the thread-safe queue so the decode worker can pick it up without data races.

462.text: Signal that all prefills are done.

464.text: The decode worker lives on the other side of that handoff, interleaving many in-flight requests while the prefill worker keeps chewing through new prompts.

466.text: A dict mapping request id to that request's in-flight decode state. This is what continuous batching looks like structurally: many requests advance one step each per pass, rather than one request running to completion.

467.text: Keep running until prefill is done and all decodes finish.

473.text: Sample the completion flag before draining the queue. Read afterwards, prefill could append its last request and set the flag in the window between drain and check, and the loop would exit having silently dropped that request, which then makes the paired comparison misalign every row after it. A one-line reordering, and the reason the result table can be trusted.

474.text: Poll the queue for any newly prefilled requests that the prefill worker has handed off for decoding.

475.text: Drain the queue, grab all available prefilled requests.

476.text: Unpack the handoff: request, KV caches, first sampled token, position.

477.text: Admit each newly prefilled request into the active set, keyed by id, with an empty output list.

478.text: Record the drained-queue state while still holding the lock, so the exit test below reasons about a consistent snapshot rather than re-reading the queue unlocked.

479.text: If nothing active and prefill not done, briefly wait.

480.text: Exit only when prefill has finished, the queue is empty, and nothing is in flight. All three conditions, evaluated against the same snapshot.

484.text: Rebuild the active set each pass rather than mutating it while iterating. Requests that finished this step simply do not get carried over.

485.text: One decode step for every in-flight request per pass. This interleaving is what the colocated arm does not do, and it is the actual mechanism behind the latency difference.

486.text: Evaluate stopping conditions for each active request: did it generate BOS (end token) or hit the maximum length?

487.text: Request finished: record timing and results.

488.text: Acquire the results lock before writing, since the main thread reads results after both workers finish.

491.text: Continue generating: append token, decode one step, sample next.

493.text: Carry the request forward with its next sampled token, again from its own generator. Which thread ran this step does not affect what was drawn.

494.text: Filter out finished requests so we only continue decoding the ones that still have tokens left to generate.

496.text: Spin up one thread for the prefill worker and one for the decode worker, which will run concurrently.

497.text: Start both workers, they run in parallel.

498.text: Launch both threads to begin parallel execution of the prefill and decode workers.

499.text: Block until both worker threads complete, ensuring all requests have finished processing before returning results.

500.text: Join the second worker thread. After this returns, all generation work is done and results are ready.

557.text: Average prompt length, needed to convert a per-token transfer cost into a per-request one.

558.text: The average TTFT advantage in milliseconds, the quantity the transfer cost has to eat before disaggregation stops paying.

567.text: The mean of the cumulative prompt length — on average, how many prompt tokens are queued ahead of a request plus its own. Because the handoff runs inline on the prefill worker, that is the number of tokens whose transfer cost each request waits behind.

568.text: Break-even: the per-token transfer cost at which the whole TTFT gain is eaten. Using the mean prompt length here instead would overstate it by roughly the queue depth, because it would charge each request only for its own tokens.

569.text: The transfer bill, totalled across the workload and already included in the disaggregated TTFT above. Not a footnote about production hardware: a charge this run actually paid.

571.text: The break-even transfer cost: the per-token price at which the advantage disappears entirely. This is the number that makes the KV handoff an engineering constraint rather than a caveat in prose.

573.text: And an invitation to falsify it — raise KV_TRANSFER_COST_MS past this value and re-run. A break-even you can cross is worth more than a claim you cannot.

576.text: The caveats, printed with the result rather than left to the reader. One worker against two, a strict-FIFO baseline with no continuous batching, and sleeps standing in for GPU time — what is being demonstrated is the scheduling structure, not a benchmark.
